{"id": "37d2051c-dfc1-4d75-8895-6a20fa45d9e8", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Since there's no existing skill on DynamoDB latency in this space, I'll note that upfront and ground my evaluation in verified AWS documentation, going through each of the four plan items. Starting with the 50ms SDK socket timeout, I'm thinking this is quite aggressive since DynamoDB p99 latency can already exceed that for many workloads, particularly strongly consistent reads.

Setting such a low timeout could cause premature retries that amplify load and worsen the exact tail latency problem it's meant to solve—AWS recommends profiling actual p99/p999 first and setting timeouts with margin using adaptive retry mode instead.

For the strongly consistent reads switch, AWS documentation is clear that these cost double the capacity and have higher latency than eventually consistent reads, so defaulting everything to strongly consistent would likely worsen p99 rather than help, and it's not even supported on GSIs.

On the DAX question, I'm considering that DAX's item cache and query cache operate separately, so running a nightly Scan wouldn't actually warm the item cache that GetItem calls rely on.

Since nightly batch scans typically have unique pagination per run, caching offers little benefit, and shoving large scan results into DAX could evict other latency-sensitive cached entries that share the cluster—better to use parallel scans, off-peak timing, or Streams/export instead of fronting a nightly Scan with DAX. On the keep-alive idea, I'm noting that SDK v3 already enables TCP keep-alive by default, making a synthetic 30-second GetItem call largely redundant.

I'll structure the response as a clear rundown of each item with its verdict—helps, hurts, or neutral—plus a concise recommendation, keeping the tone technical and organized.

"}]}

The read option is set to **eventually consistent** by default.\\\\n\\\\nThe\\xa0[GetItem](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_GetItem.html) operation provides an eventually consistent read by default. An eventually consistent read might not be able to access data immediately after the data is written to the table. To get the latest data, wait for a short amount of time, then try your read request again.\\\\n\\\\nTo retrieve the latest data as soon as the write request completes, set the **ConsistentRead** parameter to **true**. This activates strongly consistent reads. Before you activate strongly consistent reads, consider the following:\\\\n\\\\n* Strongly consistent reads might have higher latency.\\\\n* Strongly consistent reads aren\\'t supported on global secondary indexes.\\\\n* Strongly consistent reads require twice as much throughput as eventually consistent reads. Consistency model\\\\n\\\\nOne consideration for your workload is the required read consistency model following each table update. DynamoDB writes table updates in three Availability Zones in each AWS Region for durability, and all of your data usually is written in all locations in one second or less.\\\\n\\\\nDynamoDB supports three models of read consistency: eventually consistent, strongly consistent, and transactional. Unless you specify a different consistency model for your application, DynamoDB uses eventually consistent reads. If your application and users can accept eventually consistent reads where a retrieval response may occasionally produce stale data based on timing, you can provision less capacity and your costs will be the lowest of the three consistency choices.\\\\n\\\\nIf you select strongly consistent reads, DynamoDB returns a response with the most up-to-date data from all successful write operations, and your provisioned capacity and costs are higher.\\\\n\\\\nFor transactional applications where the last write must always be available for all requests, the transactional APIs are the best choice. To support transactions and simplify the developer experience of making all-or-nothing table changes, DynamoDB performs two underlying reads or writes of every item in the transaction: one to prepare the transaction and one to commit the transaction. Although the cost of each read and write is the same, this drives up the total number of reads and writes for any given transactional change, and therefore is the most expensive table update option and read consistency model\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/how-to-determine-if-amazon-dynamodb-is-appropriate-for-your-needs-and-then-plan-your-migration/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Amazon DynamoDB on Mobile \u2013 Part 2: Advanced Data Loading Options | Front-End Web & Mobile\",\"context\":\"## Consistent Reads\\\\n\\\\nBy default, all read operations, `GetItem` and `Query` included, use **eventually consistent** reads. This means that if we read the data immediately after another process modifies it, we may get the older stale data. In the case where this is not acceptable\u2014for instance, if we always wanted to make sure we have the absolute freshest data when first loading our application\u2014`GetItem` and `Query` support **consistent** reads. Enabling consistent reads is simple for both `GetItem` and `Query`.\\\\n\\\\n#### iOS\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n// GetItem\\\\nDynamoDBGetItemRequest *getItemRequest = [DynamoDBGetItemRequest new];\\\\ngetItemRequest.tableName = @\\\\\"UserTableExample\\\\\";\\\\n\\\\n// Ask for consistent reads\\\\ngetItemRequest.consistentRead = YES;\\\\n\\\\n// Configure the rest of the request\\\\n...\\\\n\\\\n// Query\\\\nDynamoDBQueryRequest *queryRequest = [DynamoDBQueryRequest new];\\\\nqueryRequest.tableName = @\\\\\"UserTableExample\\\\\";\\\\n\\\\n// Ask for consistent reads\\\\nqueryRequest.consistentRead = YES;\\\\n\\\\n// Configure the rest of the request\\\\n...\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Android\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n// GetItem with consistent reads\\\\nGetItemRequest getItemRequest = new GetItemRequest(\\\\\"UserTableExample\\\\\",key)\\\\n .withConsistentRead(true);\\\\n\\\\n// Configure the rest of the request\\\\n...\\\\n\\\\n// Query with consistent reads\\\\nQueryRequest queryRequest = new QueryRequest()\\\\n .withTableName(\\\\\"UserTableExample\\\\\")\\\\n .withConsistentRead(true);\\\\n\\\\n// Configure the rest of the request\\\\n...\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nConsistent reads are twice as expensive in terms of consumed capacity units (see the DynamoDB FAQ for an explanation of capacity units), so we recommend that you use them only when absolutely necessary\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mobile/amazon-dynamodb-on-mobile-part-2-advanced-data-loading-options/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. Understanding the differences between these caches can help you determine the performance and consistency characteristics they offer to your application.\\\\n\\\\n| Cache characteristic | Item cache | Query cache |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| Purpose | Stores the results of GetItem and BatchGetItem API operations. | Stores the results of Query and Scan API operations. These operations can return multiple items based on query conditions instead of specific item keys. |\\\\n| Access Type | Uses key-based access. When an application requests data using `GetItem` or `BatchGetItem`, DAX first checks the item cache using the primary key of the requested items. If the item is cached and unexpired, DAX returns it immediately without accessing the DynamoDB table. | Uses parameter-based access. DAX caches the result set of `Query` and `Scan` API operations. DAX serves subsequent requests with the same parameters that include the same query conditions, table, index, from the cache. This significantly reduces response times and DynamoDB read throughput consumption. |\\\\n| Cache Invalidation | DAX automatically replicates updated items into the item cache of the nodes in the DAX cluster in the following scenarios: * You write an item update through the cache. * Read an updated item version from the table. | The query cache is more challenging to invalidate than the item cache. Item updates might not directly map to cached queries or scans. You must carefully tune the query cache TTL to maintain data consistency. Writes through DAX or base table aren\\'t reflected in query cache until the TTL expires the previously cached response and DAX performs a new query against DynamoDB. |\\\\n| Global secondary index | Because the `GetItem` API operation isn\\'t supported on local secondary indexes or global secondary indexes, the item cache only caches reads from the base table. | Query cache caches queries against both tables and indexes. |\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/dax-config-considerations.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"DAX and DynamoDB consistency models\",\"context\":\"## DAX query cache behavior\\\\n\\\\nDAX caches the results from `Query` and `Scan` requests in its\\\\nquery cache. However, these results don\\'t affect the item cache at all. When your\\\\napplication issues a `Query` or `Scan` request with DAX, the\\\\nresult set is saved in the query cache\u2014not in the item cache. You can\\'t \\\\\"warm up\\\\\"\\\\nthe item cache by performing a `Scan` operation because the item cache and\\\\nquery cache are separate entities.\\\\n\\\\n### Consistency of query-update-query\\\\n\\\\nUpdates to the item cache, or to the underlying DynamoDB table, do not invalidate or\\\\nmodify the results stored in the query cache.\\\\n\\\\nTo illustrate, consider the following scenario. An application is working with the\\\\n`DocumentRevisions` table, which has `DocId` as its\\\\npartition key and `RevisionNumber` as its sort key.\\\\n\\\\n1. A client issues a `Query` for `DocId`\\\\n `101`, for all items with `RevisionNumber` greater\\\\n than or equal to `5`. DAX stores the result set in the query\\\\n cache and returns the result set to the user.\\\\n2. The client issues a `PutItem` request for `DocId`\\\\n `101` with a `RevisionNumber` value of\\\\n `20`.\\\\n3. The client issues the same `Query` as described in step 1\\\\n (`DocId`\\\\n `101` and `RevisionNumber` >=\\\\n `5`).\\\\n\\\\nIn this scenario, the cached result set for the `Query` issued in step\\\\n3 is identical to the result set that was cached in step 1. The reason is that DAX\\\\ndoes not invalidate `Query` or `Scan` result sets based on\\\\nupdates to individual items. The `PutItem` operation from step 2 is only\\\\nreflected in the DAX query cache when the TTL for the `Query`\\\\nexpires.\\\\n\\\\nYour application should consider the TTL value for the query cache and how long\\\\nyour application can tolerate inconsistent results between the query cache and the\\\\nitem cache\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.consistency.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"A walkthrough of the Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator console \u2013 Part 2 | AWS Database Blog\",\"context\":\"## **Clusters**\\\\n\\\\nDAX runs within an Amazon VPC and unless specified, the DAX cluster will run within a default VPC. This means that DAX cluster is not accessible over the Internet.\\\\n\\\\n At a high level, a DAX cluster consists of one or more nodes where one node serves as the \u2018primary\u2019 and additional nodes (if present) serve as read replicas for the cluster. A DAX cluster can support up to ten nodes per cluster (the primary node, plus a maximum of nine read replicas).\\\\n\\\\nAt runtime, the DAX client directs all of the application\u2019s DynamoDB API requests to the DAX cluster. While the application and DAX client can be configured on various compute platforms that can be accessed in a VPC like Lambda, for this example, an Amazon EC2 instance is launched into the VPC, and then the application (with the DAX client) is deployed on the EC2 instance. The application accesses DAX by specifying an endpoint for the DAX cluster. The DAX client works with the cluster endpoint to perform intelligent load-balancing and routing, so that incoming requests are evenly distributed across all the nodes in the cluster. Thus, it is very simple to implement DAX as one endpoint can handle all traffic.\\\\n\\\\nWhen you use `GetItem` with the DAX client, the request reaches DAX and if DAX can process one of these API requests directly via its cache (**cache hit**), it does so within microseconds; otherwise i.e. if the item is not available in the cache (**cache miss**), it passes the request to DynamoDB. DynamoDB returns the requested item, and DAX stores it in the item cache. Finally, the DAX cluster returns the item to the application. Also, if the DAX cluster contains more than one node, the item is replicated to all of the other nodes in the cluster. This is possible because DAX is a write-through caching service specifically designed to simplify the process of adding a cache to Amazon DynamoDB tables\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/a-walkthrough-of-the-amazon-dynamodb-accelerator-console-part-2/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. Additionally, since\\\\nDynamoDB encryption\\\\nat rest is integrated with AWS\\\\nKMS, you may experience latencies from the database having to re-establish\\\\nnew AWS KMS cache entries for each operation.\\\\n\\\\nThe easiest way to configure SDK for JavaScript to reuse TCP connections is to set the `AWS_NODEJS_CONNECTION_REUSE_ENABLED` environment variable to `1`.\\\\nThis feature was added in the 2.463.0\\\\nrelease.\\\\n\\\\nAlternatively, you can set the `keepAlive` property of an HTTP\\\\nor HTTPS agent set to `true`, as shown in the following example.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nconst AWS = require(\\'aws-sdk\\');\\\\n// http or https\\\\nconst http = require(\\'http\\');\\\\nconst agent = new http.Agent({\\\\n keepAlive: true,\\\\n// Infinity is read as 50 sockets\\\\n maxSockets: Infinity\\\\n});\\\\n\\\\nAWS.config.update({\\\\n httpOptions: {\\\\n agent\\\\n }\\\\n});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe following example shows how to set `keepAlive` for just a DynamoDB\\\\nclient:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nconst AWS = require(\\'aws-sdk\\')\\\\n// http or https\\\\nconst https = require(\\'https\\');\\\\nconst agent = new https.Agent({\\\\n keepAlive: true\\\\n});\\\\n\\\\nconst dynamodb = new AWS.DynamoDB({\\\\n httpOptions: {\\\\n agent\\\\n }\\\\n});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIf `keepAlive` is enabled, you can also set the initial delay for TCP\\\\nKeep-Alive packets with `keepAliveMsecs`, which by default is 1000ms. See\\\\nthe Node.js documentation for\\\\ndetails\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-javascript/v2/developer-guide/node-reusing-connections.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"HTTP keep-alive is on by default in modular AWS SDK for JavaScript | AWS Developer Tools Blog\",\"context\":\"## Implementation\\\\n\\\\nThe persistent connections were enabled in modular AWS SDK for JavaScript by setting up `keepAlive` by default while creating Node.js http.Agent. This is done in NodeHttpHandler internal code as follows:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nthis.httpAgent = httpAgent || new http.Agent({ keepAlive: true });\\\\nthis.httpsAgent = httpsAgent || new https.Agent({ keepAlive: true });\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAlthough not recommended, you can explicitly disable persistent connections by passing a your own httpsAgent with keepAlive not defined or set to false.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nconst { Agent } = require(\\\\\"https\\\\\");\\\\nconst { DynamoDBClient } = require(\\\\\"@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb\\\\\");\\\\nconst { NodeHttpHandler } = require(\\\\\"@aws-sdk/node-http-handler\\\\\");\\\\n\\\\nconst dynamodbClient = new DynamoDBClient({\\\\n requestHandler: new NodeHttpHandler({\\\\n httpsAgent: new Agent({ keepAlive: false }),\\\\n }),\\\\n});\\\\n```\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/developer/http-keep-alive-is-on-by-default-in-modular-aws-sdk-for-javascript/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How do I resolve the \\\\\"Signature expired\\\\\" error when I use an AWS SDK to invoke a Lambda function?\",\"context\":\"Short description\\\\n-----------------\\\\n\\\\nWhen the client time and server time don\\'t match, the Lambda signature expires, and you receive an error message similar to the following:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\"Error: native lambda error:InvalidSignatureException: Signature expired: 20230118T161739Z is now earlier than 20230118T161739Z (20190318T162239Z - 5 min.)\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nAn API request must reach AWS within 5 minutes of the timestamp in the request or AWS denies the request. In specific scenarios, you can change the client time to match the server time.\\\\n\\\\nResolution\\\\n----------\\\\n\\\\nWhen you use an AWS SDK to synchronously invoke a Lambda function, the connection lasts until the response is returned. By default, the Node.js SDK allows 50 connections. If you reach the connection quota, then the SDK queues the request locally until a connection is available. If you receive the \\\\\"Signature expired\\\\\" error and the following actions are true, then you might have reached the connection quota:\\\\n\\\\n* The Lambda function isn\\'t throttling.\\\\n* The client time is correct.\\\\n* (Node.js SDK only) You set the **correctClockSkew:true** option when you created the client to correct the time when you invoke the function.\\\\n* You invoked the Lambda function at a high rate, and the invocation runs for an extended time.\\\\n\\\\nThe SDK signs the request, and then puts the request in a queue. If the queue becomes too large and the request is pending for more than 5 minutes, then the signature expires. Because the signature expired, all additional requests fail.\\\\n\\\\nIf you don\\'t need the response from the invocation, then use [asynchronous invocation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.html). Asynchronous invocation allows the SDK to use the connection only to invoke the request and doesn\\'t wait for a response.\\\\n\\\\nYou can also use Top Level Await (TLA) in your application. Use TLA if you make API calls outside of a handler, and you receive **SignatureDoesNotMatch** exceptions when you use Node.js AWS SDK v3.\\\\n\\\\nOr, [increase the maximum number of connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-javascript/v2/developer-guide/node-configuring-maxsockets.html) that the SDK allows.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:** When you add connections, the Lambda function invokes at a higher rate and can cause throttling.\\\\n\\\\nRelated information\\\\n-------------------\\\\n\\\\n[Monitoring, debugging, and troubleshooting\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/lambda-sdk-signature\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. So here's my own assessment, grounded in AWS's documented DynamoDB/SDK v3 behavior:

**1. Set SDK socket timeout to 50 ms — risky, likely backfires**
50 ms is extremely aggressive for a *socket* (not request) timeout. If your real p99 is already north of 50 ms — which it apparently is — this setting will fire premature timeouts on normal, successful requests, not just slow ones. AWS SDK v3's default retry behavior will then retry those "failed" calls, which adds load, consumes more capacity, and can trigger a retry storm that pushes your tail latency *worse*, not better. Recommend: measure your actual latency distribution first, set the timeout with real margin above p99.9, and lean on the SDK's adaptive retry mode instead of a hard, low socket cutoff.

**2. Switch all reads to strongly consistent — will worsen p99, not fix it**
This is directly documented as counterproductive here: strongly consistent reads have *higher* latency than eventually consistent reads and consume **2x** the read capacity. They're also not supported on GSIs at all. Making this the default across all reads is very likely to raise your p99, not lower it, plus roughly double your read costs. Recommend: keep eventually consistent as default, and use `ConsistentRead: true` only on the specific paths that truly require read-after-write correctness.

**3. Put DAX in front of the nightly Scan job — low/no benefit, possible side effects**
DAX has two separate caches: an **item cache** (for GetItem/BatchGetItem) and a **query cache** (for Query/Scan). A Scan only populates the query cache, and that cache is keyed by the exact scan parameters — repeat hits only happen if you reissue the *same* scan with the *same* parameters within the TTL. A nightly full-table Scan is a one-shot, paginated traversal, so there's essentially nothing to cache-hit on the next run unless parameters are identical, and large Scan result sets sitting in the query cache can evict other entries if this DAX cluster is shared with latency-sensitive traffic. DAX is built for repeated, identical-key read patterns, not infrequent batch scans. Recommend: don't put the nightly Scan behind DAX; if it's competing with your online p99, run it with reduced parallelism/throughput (e.g., parallel Scan with a lower rate) during off-peak hours, or move it to DynamoDB Streams/incremental export instead of a full Scan.

**4. Synthetic keep-alive GetItem every 30 s — mostly redundant**
In the modular AWS SDK for JavaScript (v3), HTTP/HTTPS keep-alive is **already on by default** — the SDK reuses TCP connections for you without any extra calls. So a synthetic GetItem every 30 seconds doesn't buy you connection reuse you don't already have. There's a documented edge case where keeping traffic warm helps re-establish KMS encryption-at-rest cache entries after idle periods, so it's not purely useless — but it's a blunt, costly way to get that benefit. Recommend: tune `keepAliveMsecs`/`maxSockets` on the HTTPS agent instead of adding synthetic traffic, and only add warming calls if you've confirmed cold-cache latency after idle gaps is actually contributing to your p99.

**Bottom line:** of the four, #1 and #2 are likely to make your p99 worse, #3 won't meaningfully help a nightly Scan, and #4 is mostly solving a problem the SDK already solves by default.
